title: Red deer: nearly wiped out, back from Austria
place: First Graubünden, then most of the Swiss Alps; release in the Val Ferret (VS) in 1926
built: Almost gone by c. 1850; natural return from 1870/1872
summary: Red deer had almost disappeared from Switzerland by about 1850; after the federal hunting law of 1875 they came back on their own from Austria and Liechtenstein into Graubünden, and in 2019 Switzerland counted almost 40,000.
why: In Graubünden, red deer declined for 200 years and disappeared in the 19th century. The causes were free hunting with better guns, the cold climate of the Little Ice Age, overuse of the land by a growing population, and conflicts with food and wood production. By about 1850, red deer had almost gone from Switzerland.

The federal hunting law of 1875 gave better protection. From 1872, red deer came back on their own from Vorarlberg, Liechtenstein and North and South Tyrol into Graubünden. From 1905 they were hunted again officially. In 1926, two stags and three hinds (females) were released in the Val Ferret (VS).

Red deer now live again in almost all cantons, mostly in Graubünden, Valais and Ticino. In 2019 Switzerland counted almost 40,000. Graubünden plans its hunt so that the numbers stay at a level that the forest and farmland can carry.
gained: The largest wild animal of the Alps lives again in almost all cantons of Switzerland.
Graubünden thinks that a spring population of 13,000 to 14,000 red deer is sustainable. Such a population has 4,500 to 5,000 calves per year, so hunting is needed every year.
lost: Until the 1970s, red deer numbers in Graubünden repeatedly went above what the habitat could carry.
Without hunting, red deer would cause large damage in forests and on farmland, and many would die in winter.

title: Federal hunting reserves: chamois and roe deer come back
place: 43 federal hunting reserves, mostly in the Alps (oldest protected mountain: Kärpf, GL)
built: Federal hunting law and first reserves 1875; roe deer back on the Plateau by c. 1920
summary: By 1875 roe deer, chamois, red deer and ibex had almost gone; the first federal hunting law of 1875 limited hunting and created federal hunting reserves, and chamois and roe deer recovered strongly.
why: By the middle of the 19th century, the wild hoofed animals had almost gone: roe deer, chamois, red deer and ibex. Better guns and the destruction of forests were the causes. In 1875, the extinction of the chamois seemed to be only a question of time.

The federal hunting law of 17 September 1875 limited the hunt of large game to 14 days. It banned the shooting of mothers and young animals. It also created federal hunting reserves, some larger than 100 km². In them all game except predators was strictly protected. Game wardens fought poaching (illegal hunting).

The law worked. The chamois spread again. The roe deer came back from southern Germany. By about 1920 it lived in most of the Jura and the Plateau, and in 1930 it reached the edge of the Alps. Today 43 federal hunting reserves exist.
gained: The reserves were starting points for the recovery. The first ibex colonies were also set up in them.
Today about 135,000 roe deer and about 90,000 chamois live in Switzerland. Roe deer live again everywhere up to the tree line.
Some protected mountains are very old. The people of Glarus banned hunting on the Kärpf in 1548, and it is still a protected 'Freiberg' today.
lost: The 1875 law did not protect predators. Bear, wolf, lynx, otter, eagle and bearded vulture were still hunted and wiped out.
Today many deer and chamois populations are high or too high. This causes damage to forests. In 1962 the law already had to add rules against wildlife damage.
Roe deer like to eat young trees such as silver fir. This tree is very important in protection forests (forests that protect against avalanches and rockfall).

title: Alpine ibex: hunted out, then reintroduced
place: Swiss Alps and Jura; first release in the Weisstannental (SG)
built: Extinct in the 19th century; reintroduced from 1911
summary: People hunted the Alpine ibex out of Switzerland in the 19th century; from 1911, ibex bred in St. Gallen from Italian stock were released, and today about 15,000 to 16,000 live here.
why: For centuries people hunted the ibex hard. People believed that its horns could heal illness. The ibex left Graubünden in the 17th century. The Canton of St. Gallen says that the last ibex in Switzerland was shot in 1809. Only a small group survived in the Gran Paradiso, a royal hunting ground in Italy.

In 1906, young ibex were smuggled from Italy into Switzerland. The Wildpark Peter und Paul in St. Gallen bred them. On 8 May 1911, the first ibex went free in the Weisstannental (SG). From 1920, ibex from this breeding were also released in the Swiss National Park. The first colonies were placed in federal hunting reserves (areas where hunting is banned).

The colonies grew. Today about 15,000 to 16,000 ibex live in Switzerland. In some colonies the high numbers harmed other species and the vegetation. So the numbers are now regulated. Graubünden has hunted the protected ibex selectively (only chosen animals) since 1977.
gained: A native animal came back to the Alps. The Swiss National Park calls the rescue of the ibex a success story that is unique in the world.
The federal inventory now lists 41 colony areas in the Alps and the Jura. They form the basis for counting and for hunting plans.
lost: Before 1911 the ibex had been absent from Switzerland for about 100 years. Its use as a medicine and free hunting caused this.
In some colonies, many ibex had negative effects on other species and on vegetation. So people now shoot some of them each year.

title: Atlantic salmon: lost behind the dams
place: High Rhine from Basel to the Rhine Falls and its tributaries (Aare, Reuss, Birs, Wiese, Ergolz)
built: lost in the 20th century; releases since 1984
summary: River works, pollution and above all hydropower dams on the Rhine and Aare cut the salmon's way from the sea, so it disappeared from Switzerland in the 20th century.
why: For thousands of years, salmon swam from the North Sea up the Rhine to spawn (lay eggs) in Swiss rivers. Their main area reached up to the Rhine Falls. The salmon was still common in large parts of the Swiss Rhine basin until the end of the 19th century.

Large river corrections, more water pollution, overfishing and above all the building of river power stations on the Rhine and the Aare broke the migration. The adult fish could no longer swim back up, and the salmon disappeared in the 20th century.

Basel started a salmon rearing programme in the Lange Erlen in 1984. Today young salmon are released in Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft and Aargau, and the federal office BAFU pays 40 % and coordinates the work.
gained: The river power stations produce electricity. For example, the federal power station list gives Augst (1912) and Birsfelden (1955) on the Rhine near Basel.
Since 2011 the water protection law asks that fish migration be restored at all Swiss hydropower plants by 2030. River restorations on the Birs (2004) and the lower Wiese (2018) made new habitat.
lost: A large migratory fish of the Rhine disappeared from Switzerland in the 20th century.

Salmon cannot yet return to Basel on their own. In 2019, the French power stations at Rhinau, Marckolsheim and Vogelgrün still blocked the way between Strasbourg and Basel, so the 2020 goal was missed.

title: White stork: gone by 1950, back from Altreu
place: Altreu near Selzach (SO), on the Aare in the Witi plain; today storks breed across the Swiss lowlands
summary: The white stork stopped breeding in Switzerland by 1950, and a project started at Altreu in 1948 brought it back to over 500 pairs.
why: Farming became more intensive in the 20th century. Fields were drained and farmers used more pesticides. The stork lost wet meadows where it finds food. By 1950 not a single stork pair bred in Switzerland.
In 1948, Max Bloesch started a stork station in Altreu (SO), on the Aare. From 1955 he and his friends imported young storks from Algeria several times.
Altreu became the centre of the comeback. The federal office for the environment (BAFU) still pays for stork support, for example wet 'stork meadows' in the Witi near Altreu.
gained: The stork breeds again in all of Switzerland. In 2021 the Swiss population was over 500 brood pairs, and Altreu is still the largest colony.
In 2008 the foundation EURO-NATUR named Altreu a 'stork village of Europe'.
New wet meadows for storks also help other animals: wading birds rest there and rare toads and tree frogs spawn there.
lost: The original Swiss breeding population disappeared completely by 1950. Part of the new population comes from young storks imported from Algeria.
The wet meadows that storks need were largely drained for farming. Today some of them are made again with pumps and seals.

title: Whitefish species lost in over-fertilised lakes
place: Swiss lakes, for example Lake Constance, Lake Zug, Lake Geneva and Walensee
summary: At least 30 % of the whitefish species of Swiss lakes died out, mostly in lakes that were over-fertilised by people in the second half of the 20th century.
why: Swiss lakes once held at least 34 whitefish species (Felchen, a salmon-like fish of open and deep water). They exist nowhere else in the world. Today 24 remain.

In the second half of the 20th century, sewage and farming brought large amounts of nutrients into many lakes (eutrophication). Bacteria then used up the oxygen in deep water. Species that laid their eggs on the deep lake floor in summer and autumn died out.

Sewage treatment plants later lowered the phosphorus again, for example in Walensee. In lakes that stayed nutrient-poor, such as Lake Lucerne, Lake Brienz and Lake Thun, all known whitefish species still live.
gained: Cleaner lakes after sewage treatment: Walensee is nutrient-poor again since the 1990s.
Whitefish are still the main catch of Swiss fishers: on average 60 % of the commercial catch and 25 % of the anglers' catch in the last two decades.
lost: Whole species are gone, for example the Kilch of Lake Constance, the Zuger Albock and the Zuger Albeli of Lake Zug. In Lake Zug only one of three whitefish species survived.
About one third of the Kilch's genes survive only mixed into the other whitefish of Lake Constance.
Lakes with fewer species give a smaller whitefish catch per unit of phosphorus than lakes that kept their variety.

title: Peregrine falcon: DDT, ban and comeback
place: All of Switzerland; strongest losses outside the Alps and in the Jura
built: decline from 1950; ban of DDT in the 1970s
summary: The pesticide DDT almost wiped out the peregrine falcon outside the Alps, and after DDT was banned the bird came back to about 300 pairs.
why: From 1950, farmers used the pesticide DDT. Peregrine falcons took in the poison with their prey. Like other birds of prey, they then laid eggs with shells that were too thin, and breeding success fell to almost zero.
In 1971, only one successful brood pair was found outside the Alps. DDT was banned in the 1970s, and the slow recovery began.
Since about 2009, new threats appeared. Some pigeon breeders poisoned falcons with pigeons prepared with nerve poison. A court convicted one pigeon breeder in 2016.
gained: After the ban, the falcon came back. Today the Swiss population is estimated at about 300 pairs.
Falcons nest again in cities, for example at a nest site with a webcam at the Josefstrasse in Zürich.
lost: Between the 1950s and the 1970s the bird almost disappeared from the Swiss lowlands and the Jura.

Since the recovery, numbers fall again: about 20 % fewer birds in the Jura in recent years. The Vogelwarte now lists the falcon as 'vulnerable' on the Red List. Reasons include illegal poisoning, the growing eagle owl population and disturbance at breeding cliffs.

title: Eurasian beaver: hunted out, then reintroduced
place: Rivers and lakes of the Plateau, Valais and Graubünden; first release on the Versoix (GE)
built: Extinct in the early 19th century; 141 animals released 1956–1977
summary: People hunted the beaver out of Switzerland by the early 19th century; from 1956 to 1977, 141 beavers were released, and in 2022 about 4,900 lived in Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
why: People hunted the beaver for its dense fur, for its meat and for castoreum (a scent from a gland, used as a medicine). The BAFU report says that direct persecution caused the loss, not the straightening of rivers. The last beaver in Switzerland was killed at the start of the 19th century.

From 1956, a group around Maurice Blanchet and Robert Hainard released the first 8 beavers on the Versoix (GE). In the 1960s and 1970s, other private people and cantonal hunting offices followed. By 1977, 141 beavers from France, Norway and the Soviet Union had been released. More than 40% of them were later found dead.

The beaver then spread along the large rivers. A national survey in winter 2022 counted 1,382 territories in Switzerland. It estimated about 4,900 beavers in Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Conflicts also grow, mainly in farming areas.
gained: Beavers build dams and change streams. In 2022 the survey found 1,316 beaver dams; in 2008 there were only 185.
The 2022 report says the beaver helps biodiversity, water retention and water quality. It can be used on purpose for nature protection.
lost: Switzerland had no beavers from the early 19th century until 1956.
Of the 141 released beavers, 59 were found dead. Only 82 became founders of the new population.
Beaver activity causes conflicts, mainly in farming zones. The 2022 report says that new tools are needed to solve them in the long term.

title: Eurasian lynx: wiped out, then reintroduced
place: Releases in Obwalden and at the Creux-du-Van (NE); today in the Alps and the Jura
built: Extinct in the 19th century; reintroduced from 1971
summary: Forest clearing and hunting wiped out the lynx in the 19th century; from 1971, lynx from the Carpathians were released in Obwalden and Neuchâtel, and in 2018 BAFU estimated about 300 lynx in Switzerland.
why: Lynx once lived in all of Switzerland. People cut the forests for farming, and the lynx lost its habitat. Excessive hunting in the 19th century then wiped it out.

Switzerland protected the lynx in 1962. In 1967 the Federal Council approved its return. Lynx from the Carpathians were released in 1971 in the Grosses Melchtal (OW), in 1972 in the Chlischlierental (OW) and in 1974 and 1975 at the Creux-du-Van (NE). Private people also released lynx. In total, 25 to 30 lynx were released in the 1970s.

From 2001 to 2008, lynx from the Jura and the north-western Alps were moved to make the Alpine population stronger. In 2018, BAFU estimated about 300 lynx: about 200 in the Alps and Prealps and about 100 in the Jura.
gained: The lynx hunts roe deer and chamois. BAFU says that this helps the natural regrowth of the forest.
Switzerland now has the only large, connected lynx populations of the Alpine region.
lost: All Swiss lynx come from only 10 to 20 founder animals. They have lost genetic diversity, and inbreeding (breeding between close relatives) occurs.
Lynx kill an estimated 20 to 50 farm animals per year. Illegal killing of lynx still happens.
Since 2012 the hunting ordinance allows the regulation of lynx where they strongly reduce roe deer and chamois.

title: Wild boar: hunted out, back on its own
place: Jura, Plateau, parts of the Prealps, Rhone valley and Ticino
built: Extinct by the early 19th century; natural return in the 20th century, strong increase from 1980
summary: Hunting wiped out the wild boar in Switzerland by the early 19th century; in the 20th century it came back on its own from the north and west, and since 1980 its numbers have risen strongly.
why: In earlier centuries, the authorities paid bounties for killing animals that people saw as harmful, such as bears, wolves and wild boar. BAFU says that excessive hunting in the 19th century wiped out the wild boar in Switzerland.

The Canton of Solothurn says that wild boar were wiped out in the 18th and 19th centuries. In the 20th century they came back on their own from the north and the west. Only from 1980 did their numbers rise clearly.
Today wild boar live mainly in the Jura, on the Plateau, in parts of the Prealps, in the Rhone valley and in parts of Ticino. With a milder climate, they will also live higher in the Alps.
gained: A native wild animal lives again in large parts of Switzerland.
lost: Wild boar damage maize, wheat, rapeseed and above all grassland. In Solothurn, 80–90% of the damage is on grassland. Numbers and damage still tend to rise.
Wild boar and domestic pigs are close relatives. So classical and African swine fever can pass between them.

title: Bearded vulture: wiped out and brought back
place: Swiss Alps; release sites in the Swiss National Park (GR), the Calfeisental (SG) and at Melchsee-Frutt (OW)
built: wiped out by c. 1900; releases from 1991
summary: People shot and poisoned the bearded vulture until it was gone from the Alps, and from 1991 released young birds bred in zoos bring it back.
why: In the 19th century, people believed that the bearded vulture (a very large bird that eats bones of dead animals) killed lambs, goats and even children. Guns and high shooting rewards (bounties) led to its extermination in the Alps in the early 20th century. Today it is known that the bird is not a hunter.
In Valais, one of the last birds was found dead near Visp in February 1886, next to a poisoned fox carcass. The last proven brood in Valais was in 1891.

From 1991, a foundation (today Stiftung Pro Bartgeier) released young birds from breeding stations. The first releases were in the Swiss National Park, with permission from the Federal Council. Later releases were in the Calfeisental (2010–2014) and at Melchsee-Frutt (since 2015).
gained: The bird breeds again in Switzerland. The first two wild pairs bred in 2007, near the Ofenpass and near La Punt.
By the end of 2023, 53 birds had been released in Switzerland and 163 young had hatched in the wild. Brood pairs had settled in 30 territories.
In 2025, 26 young birds left the nest in Switzerland. The release site at Melchsee-Frutt has an information stand for visitors every summer.
lost: The original Alpine population was lost completely. The new population comes from few founder birds, so its genetic diversity (variety of genes) is very low.
The birds still face risks from people: disturbance at nests, collisions with cables and wind turbines, and poisoning.

title: Wolf: persecuted to extinction, back on its own since 1995
place: Whole Switzerland; return first in Valais (Val Ferret), first pack at the Calanda (GR)
built: Gone by c. 1870–1890; natural return from 1995
summary: Wolves were hunted out of Switzerland in the 19th century; from 1995 single wolves came back on their own from Italy and France, the first pack formed in 2012, and on 1 February 2026 there were 30 Swiss and 10 cross-border packs.
why: Forests were cut and wild prey became rare. So wolves ate farm animals, and people hunted them even more. In many regions everyone had the right, often the duty, to kill wolves. Reliable traps and strychnine (a poison) came in the 19th century.

The wolf disappeared region by region: from Zurich around 1684, from Valais in 1870, from Ticino in 1872 and from Solothurn in 1874. In the Ajoie (Jura), wolves were seen until 1890. Single wolves still came later. For example, a wolf was shot at Eischoll (VS) in 1947.

From 1995, single wolves came back on their own from Italy and France. In 1995 and 1996, one or two wolves killed many sheep in the Val Ferret and the Val d'Entremont (VS). Genetic tests showed that they came from the Italian population. In 2012, the first pack (family group) formed at the Calanda (GR).
gained: BAFU calls the return of this large predator a success of species protection. Wolves mainly eat roe deer, chamois and red deer.
lost: Wolves also kill farm animals. Herd protection is necessary. The federal government gives about 10 million francs per year for it and pays 80% of the compensation for killed farm animals.

Wolf packs are now regulated (some wolves are shot) when other measures are not enough. BAFU says this slowed the fast growth of the population. The spread of the wolf causes dispute, also between hunters and nature protection.

title: Brown bear: last one shot in 1904, visitors since 2005
place: Lower Engadine, Val Müstair, Swiss National Park and Puschlav (GR)
built: Last bear shot 1904; single bears come back since 2005
summary: The last Swiss bear was shot in the Val S-charl in 1904; since 2005, single young bears come on their own from the Trentino into Graubünden, but no population has formed.
why: People hunted bears hard in the 18th and 19th centuries. The canton paid a bounty (a reward) for every bear shot. On 1 September 1904, the hunters Padruot Fried and Jon Sarott Bischoff shot the last Swiss bear on the Piz Pisoc above the Val S-charl.

A small native population survived in the Trentino in Italy. Between 1999 and 2002, ten bears were released in the Adamello-Brenta park there. In late July 2005, a young male came from the Trentino via South Tyrol into Switzerland. For two months it roamed the Val Müstair, the Swiss National Park and the Lower Engadine.

Switzerland did not reintroduce bears. The bear has been protected since 1962, but the federal bear concept says that human safety always comes first. In February 2013 the bear M13 was shot in the Puschlav. It searched for food in villages and followed people.
gained: Bears come back on their own. In the last quarter of 2025, Graubünden received 13 bear reports, and at times two bears were in the canton.
In surveys the bear does better than the wolf and the lynx, a KORA zoologist said in 2004.
lost: The first bear of 2005 killed a calf and about two dozen sheep.
Bears that lose their fear of people are shot. Under the bear concept, catching and keeping them in an enclosure is never an option.

title: Eurasian otter: eradicated on purpose, back since 2009
place: Lake Neuchâtel (last signs 1989); return on the Rhine and Inn (GR) and the Aare near Bern
summary: From 1888 the federal state paid bounties to eradicate the otter; after the last signs in 1989 Switzerland had no wild otters until one was filmed in 2009, and otters now breed again on the Inn and the Aare.
why: In the middle of the 19th century, more than 1,000 otters lived in Switzerland. Fishermen saw them as pests. In 1888, a federal fishery law aimed to wipe out the otter and other fish predators with bounty payments. By 1917, 2,000 otters had been killed.

The otter was protected in 1952, but it declined further. From the 1940s, rivers were canalized, piped underground or used for hydropower, and pollution grew. In 1975 only about 15 otters were left. A release of 8 otters from Bulgaria in the Schwarzwasser area (BE) failed. In 1989 the last signs were found at Lake Neuchâtel.

In 2009, a camera in a fish pass on the Rhine in Graubünden filmed an otter. Otters came back on their own from France and Austria. In 2017, a female with a cub was photographed near Samedan on the Inn: the first natural breeding since 1989. On the Aare near Bern, a small group lives since otters escaped from a zoo during a flood in 2005.
gained: Otters recovered in Europe thanks to nature protection and the ban of harmful pesticides. Since 2009 they have been seen again on the Inn, Ticino, Hinterrhein, Rhone and Aare.
lost: Roads cut the routes of otters along rivers, and many otters die in traffic. Fish traps without otter guards also kill them.
Otters sometimes take fish from fish ponds, which causes economic damage.
